cards.title: A job is progress in a circumstance, not a customer type
cards.summary: Define jobs as the functional, social and emotional progress someone seeks in a specific circumstance, rather than as demographic segments.
cards.use_when: Starting any avatar or customer-research effort and deciding what unit of analysis to research and record.
steps: State the job as progress-in-a-circumstance: 'when [situation], I want to [progress], so I can [outcome]'.
Include all three dimensions: what the person is trying to accomplish functionally, how they want to be seen (social), and how they want to feel (emotional).
Reject substitutes that are demographics-only: age, gender, income or a stock-photo persona with no causal mechanism does not define who buys or why.
Treat the circumstance as the driver of the decision; the same person can hire different solutions in different situations.
Test the definition by asking whether it explains why a real customer chose this and not an alternative in that moment.
caveats: Demographics can still be used for media buying or reach planning, but they do not explain the choice and should not be the avatar's core.
A job statement without a circumstance usually collapses back into a generic persona.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Mine five sources for undiscovered jobs
cards.summary: Find jobs by looking in personal life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses rather than asking customers for feature ideas.
cards.use_when: When you need new job candidates rather than validation of existing assumptions or feature wishlists.
steps: Personal life: look outside the product category at routines and struggles in everyday life that your product could serve.
Nonconsumption: study people who currently buy nothing in the category and find out what they do instead.
Workarounds and compensating behaviors: watch for duct-tape solutions, spreadsheets, manual steps and homemade fixes that reveal an unmet job.
Negative jobs: identify tasks people hate doing or dread and would gladly hand off.
Unusual uses: examine off-label and edge-case uses of the product; they often expose a job the product was not designed for.
For each candidate, record quoted evidence from the person and the trigger circumstance, not just the inferred need.
caveats: Feature-request surveys and focus groups asking what to add produce wishlists, not jobs; they miss the context that causes purchase.
Off-label use signals a possible job, but confirm it recurs before treating it as a segment.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Prioritize passive struggle data over active operational data
cards.summary: Favor observations of customer struggle over sales and customer-attribute reports, which are easier to collect but describe outcomes rather than causes.
cards.use_when: When choosing what evidence to gather and when a data-driven team wants to substitute reports for direct research.
steps: Recognize the fallacy of active data: sales figures, CRM fields and customer characteristics are readily available and tend to crowd out the harder-to-get data about why people acted.
Treat sales and attribute data as outcome evidence: useful for sizing and segmentation, but not for explaining the causal mechanism of choice.
Collect passive data of struggle: what the customer tried, what frustrated them, what they rigged up, and what finally triggered the switch.
Record the struggle in the customer's own words so the avatar rests on quoted evidence.
Use quantitative data afterward to check whether the discovered job is common enough to matter.
caveats: This is not a rejection of analytics; it is a warning about using convenient operational data to answer causal questions.
Small qualitative samples can reveal a job but cannot establish its prevalence without follow-up measurement.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Map the forces: push and pull versus habits and anxieties
cards.summary: A purchase happens when the push of the struggle and the pull of the new solution outweigh the habits of the present and the anxiety of the new.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing why prospects stall or abandon, or when building objection-handling into an avatar record.
steps: Identify the push: the frustration or triggering event that makes the current situation untenable.
Identify the pull: the attractiveness of the new solution and the progress it promises.
Identify the habits of the present: routines, sunk costs and defaults that keep the customer using the old approach.
Identify the anxieties of the new: fear of the unknown, risk of looking foolish, switching cost, data-migration worry, uncertainty that it will work.
Judge relative magnitude: if pull is weak or anxiety and habit are strong, the purchase does not happen even when the customer wants the outcome.
Record opposing forces as objections to address later in page or offer design; the avatar's job is to name them, not resolve them here.
caveats: Addressing objections on the page belongs to landing-page and offer work; this section only discovers and documents them.
Strong anxiety is not the same as low desire; a customer can want the progress and still not switch.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Interview by reconstructing the purchase timeline
cards.summary: Interview technique that traces the chain of triggers and events leading to a decision instead of asking about product attributes or satisfaction.
cards.use_when: Running customer interviews to uncover the job and the trigger moment behind a purchase.
steps: Ask the customer to tell the story of how they came to buy, starting before they knew your product existed.
Track the timeline: the first thought something had to change, the events in between, and the moment of decision.
Probe for the trigger event: what specifically happened that made the status quo unacceptable that week or that day.
Ask what they tried before, what they almost bought, and what they turned down, to surface competing solutions.
Avoid attribute questions such as 'which feature did you like' or hypotheticals such as 'would you buy this'; they generate rationalizations rather than stories.
Capture verbatim quotes at each stage so the avatar record carries evidence rather than summary.
caveats: Retrospective accounts are imperfect; ask for concrete events and sequences to reduce post-hoc rationalization.
Do not lead the customer toward the answer you want; let the timeline reveal the cause.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Distinguish the Big Hire from the Little Hire
cards.summary: Separate the purchase decision from the actual use and repeat-use decision, because a good job on the buying side does not guarantee retention.
cards.use_when: When diagnosing whether problems sit in acquisition or in onboarding, activation and repeat usage.
steps: Define the Big Hire as the moment of purchase or signup: what triggered it, what was compared, what anxiety was overcome.
Define the Little Hire as each subsequent decision to actually use and keep using the product.
Interview separately for each: the Big Hire timeline often differs from the Little Hire experience.
Look for mismatch: a customer may buy enthusiastically and then never activate, signalling the job promised at purchase was not the job they experienced.
Record both in the avatar: the buying job and the using job, with their distinct triggers and obstacles.
caveats: Confusing the two produces avatars that explain acquisition but not retention, or vice versa.
A strong Big Hire can mask a broken Little Hire for months before churn shows up.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Build the job spec: tradeoffs, competition and obstacles
cards.summary: A job spec is the résumé of experiences a solution must deliver, defining which tradeoffs the customer accepts, what alternatives must be beaten, and what obstacles must be removed.
cards.use_when: After a job is identified, when translating it into requirements for product, offer or messaging.
steps: List the tradeoffs the customer is willing to make, and those they are not; these bound acceptable solutions.
Identify the competing solutions that must be beaten in the customer's mind, including doing nothing, workarounds and adjacent products.
List the obstacles that must be removed before the customer can make progress, both practical and emotional.
Express the spec as the sequence of experiences the customer expects, in the order they encounter them.
Use the spec as the yardstick for product, offer and message decisions rather than adding features by request.
caveats: A spec describes experiences, not a feature list; converting it into features is product work that follows.
The spec changes when the circumstance changes, so re-check it against new interview evidence.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Storyboard the customer's struggle
cards.summary: Visualize the sequence of a customer's struggle and choices to expose where the current situation breaks down and where your solution enters.
cards.use_when: Synthesizing interview material into a shared internal view of the job before writing avatar records or messaging.
steps: Lay out the timeline as scenes: first thought of change, search, consideration, purchase, first use, repeat use.
At each scene, note what the customer did, felt, said and worried about.
Mark the trigger moment where the status quo became unacceptable.
Mark the points of anxiety and the moments of habit that nearly stopped the decision.
Mark where competing solutions, including doing nothing, appeared.
Use the storyboard to check that your avatar record, offer and messaging address the actual sequence rather than an assumed funnel.
caveats: The storyboard is a synthesis artifact, not a substitute for raw quotes and evidence.
Resist smoothing the story into a tidy funnel; the messy path is where the insight lives.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Give every avatar quoted evidence
cards.summary: A non-negotiable baseline for avatar records: direct quotes from research that support the job, the trigger and the objections.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing avatar records, especially when tempted to summarize without evidence.
steps: Attach at least one verbatim quote to each key claim: the job, the circumstance, the trigger and the opposing forces.
Keep quotes specific and contextual; a quote about a feeling or a workaround is more useful than a quote about liking the brand.
Note the source of each quote, such as an interview or an observation, so the record can be traced.
Remove or flag claims with no supporting quote rather than smoothing them into confident prose.
Use the quotes in downstream messaging as raw language the market actually uses.
caveats: Quotes can be edited for clarity but not for meaning; preserving the customer's phrasing is much of the value.
A single quote illustrates a job; it does not prove prevalence.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Inventory candidates before fixing the number of avatars
cards.summary: Research should produce a discovered set of jobs from interviews and observations rather than a predetermined count of personas.
cards.use_when: Planning avatar research and deciding how many distinct avatars to maintain.
steps: Collect job candidates from the five mining sources: personal life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses.
Cluster candidates by the circumstance and progress sought, not by demographics.
Merge clusters that differ only superficially; keep clusters that involve genuinely different tradeoffs, triggers or obstacles.
Keep the volume of avatars in a sensible operating range so the library stays usable rather than becoming a folder of near-duplicates.
Revisit the set as new interview evidence arrives; avatars can be added, split or retired.
caveats: No fixed number of avatars is universal; the right count depends on how many distinct jobs exist in your market.
Each retained avatar should carry the same evidence standard, so the set stays comparable.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use negative jobs as an opportunity lens
cards.summary: Tasks people dread doing are strong job candidates because removing an unpleasant obligation is a clear progress worth paying for.
cards.use_when: When hunting for new offers or messaging angles, especially in categories where customers complain about the process rather than the product.
steps: Ask what part of the process customers visibly procrastinate over, complain about or delegate whenever possible.
Distinguish dread from mere inconvenience: a negative job involves reluctance and avoidance, not just time cost.
Find the workaround people use to avoid the task, such as paying someone else, batching it, or ignoring it entirely.
Test whether removing that task is the real promise: 'you never have to do X' may beat feature comparisons.
Record the negative job with a quote describing the dread in the customer's own words.
caveats: Negative jobs still require a trigger to activate the purchase; discomfort alone does not cause switching.
Removing a task can reduce perceived value for some buyers who take pride in doing it themselves.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Diagnose a stalled decision with the competing-solutions list
cards.summary: Identify every alternative the customer weighed, including doing nothing and DIY fixes, to find which one actually wins and why.
cards.use_when: When conversion is weak or customers describe long deliberation before buying.
steps: Ask the customer what they almost bought or did instead, and what made them hesitate.
Include non-obvious competitors: doing nothing, a spreadsheet, an intern, an agency, a template, a friend's advice, or a different category entirely.
For each alternative, record the advantage the customer saw in it, such as price, familiarity or lower risk.
Identify the specific advantage your solution must have to beat the winning alternative.
Feed the resulting comparison into the avatar record as evidence of the real competitive set.
caveats: The customer's mental competitive set often differs from the industry's own competitive map.
Doing nothing is frequently the strongest competitor and is easy to overlook.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Capture trigger moments as discrete, datable events
cards.summary: A trigger is a specific event that made the status quo unacceptable, and pinpointing it beats recording vague motivations.
cards.use_when: When your avatar or messaging lacks urgency and prospects agree with the message but never act.
steps: Ask what changed in the week or month before the purchase: a move, a hire, a failed task, a deadline, an incident.
Write the trigger as a concrete event with a rough date rather than a general condition such as 'wanted to grow'.
Check how much time elapsed between trigger and purchase; a long gap suggests unresolved anxiety or habit.
Use the trigger to time messaging and offers rather than presenting always-on urgency that means nothing.
Record the trigger in the avatar as part of the job statement's circumstance.
caveats: Some categories have recurring triggers rather than one dramatic event; record the pattern, not a fabricated story.
Correlation between an event and purchase in one interview does not establish it as the general trigger.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Treat habits of the present as the silent competitor
cards.summary: The customer's existing routine and defaults block change even when the new solution is clearly better, so map the habit before assuming desire is enough.
cards.use_when: When prospects acknowledge the problem and the solution yet fail to switch.
steps: Identify what the customer currently does and what makes it easy, such as existing workflow, learned skill or a sunk-cost tool.
Ask what would have to change in their routine for adoption, and who else would be affected.
Look for frictionless switch mechanisms: import tools, migration help, templates, guided onboarding, a service that does the setup.
Estimate the strength of the habit against the strength of the push; if habit is strong, reduce friction rather than amplify messaging.
Record the habit in the avatar as an obstacle to be removed, not an objection to be argued away.
caveats: More persuasive claims do not overcome a strong habit; friction removal usually matters more.
Some habits represent genuine preference and should be respected rather than attacked.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Study nonconsumption to find latent demand
cards.summary: People who buy nothing in the category are a rich source of jobs because their current coping mechanisms reveal unmet progress.
cards.use_when: When the existing market is crowded and growth requires serving buyers the category has never reached.
steps: Define nonconsumers as people with the struggle who currently purchase no solution, including those who have never bought in the category.
Interview them about how they cope: manual methods, avoidance, borrowing from friends, or living with the problem.
Identify why the category is invisible or unacceptable to them: price, complexity, distrust, or identity.
Find the progress they want that no current product frames itself around.
Record the nonconsumption job separately from existing-customer jobs, since triggers and objections differ.
caveats: Nonconsumers may be hard to recruit through normal customer channels; use referrals and community contexts.
Serving nonconsumers often requires rethinking the offer and the entry point, not just the message.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Use unusual uses as a research probe, not an instant segment
cards.summary: Off-label and edge-case uses point to jobs the product was not designed for; validate the recurring pattern before acting on it.
cards.use_when: When reviewing support tickets, reviews or usage data and finding customers using the product in unexpected ways.
steps: Scan reviews, support conversations and community posts for uses outside the intended purpose.
Ask those customers what they were trying to accomplish and what triggered the need for the workaround use.
Check how many other customers show the same pattern before promoting it to a job or avatar.
Assess whether serving the pattern requires product change or only clearer framing and positioning.
If the pattern recurs, record it as a job with quotes and triggers like any other avatar.
caveats: One creative customer is an anecdote, not a market; recurrence is the test.
Pursuing every unusual use fragments focus and can dilute the core job.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Avoid persona theater: no demographic avatars without a job
cards.summary: Avatars built from demographic fields or fictional characters with stock photos do not explain behavior and should not be produced.
cards.use_when: When reviewing existing persona documents or when a stakeholder asks for an age-and-income-based avatar template.
steps: Check whether the avatar defines a circumstance and progress sought; if it only lists age, gender and income, it is not usable for decision-making.
Replace demographic descriptors with the job statement and the quotes supporting it.
If demographics are retained for media targeting, keep them in a separate layer, clearly marked as reach criteria rather than motivation.
Test the avatar by asking whether it predicts what a customer will do next and what they will object to.
Retire avatar documents that cannot answer those questions.
caveats: Demographic data still has legitimate uses in media buying, audience sizing and compliance; the objection is to using it as the causal explanation.
Fictional characters can be useful for communication and empathy, but only when built on real evidence rather than invented.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx

cards.title: Ask what the customer fired, not only what they hired
cards.summary: The job includes what the customer stopped using, and knowing what got dismissed shows the tradeoffs and loyalties at stake.
cards.use_when: When mapping the competitive set and understanding what switching away from a solution really costs the customer.
steps: Ask what they were using before and what finally made them abandon it.
Probe for emotional and social cost of switching, such as embarrassment about the old choice or reluctance to let a relationship go.
Note whether the fired solution was a product, a person, a service or a habit.
Identify what would make the customer fire your product next; that is your retention risk.
Record both the hire and the fire in the avatar so downstream offers reflect the real tradeoff.
caveats: Customers may underreport what they fire out of politeness or loyalty; cross-check with the timeline.
In B2B contexts, firing a solution can involve relationships and politics beyond the product.
cards.source_name: Competing Against Luck_ The Story of Innovation and Customer Choice (1).docx
